correctness.rationale: The up-cone equality implies monotonicity and maps source maxima to target maxima. For a nonsingleton last target level, an earlier point mapped to a maximal v would force the last source level to map constantly to v, and then every earlier point, being below the last level, has image at most v. This last inference rules out attaining a different maximal value even on the same earlier level. Consequently the last source level alone covers the last target level, and lower back witnesses all stay in the lower prefix. An optional extra value encodes omitted elements of a truncated last level, giving the T weight. For a singleton top v above a nonempty target prefix, the last source level is all v and the last source level with a non-v image is some t<i. Restrict to that level's non-v points and all earlier levels; this preserves all lower back witnesses. Extension by v is inverse and every retained point sees a later v witness. A one-point target and the virtual empty-prefix cases give the stated bases. Prefix sums give the stated complexity in the specified arithmetic model. The frozen artifacts/check_pmorph.py exists; reading it confirms it compares the tables against the exact up-cone definition, but the recorded 687-case output was not counted as independent replay. A separate implementation checked 65 small vector pairs by exhaustive function enumeration and checked the two W(3,3) examples by 729 functions each, obtaining 12 and 6. This is bounded corroboration, not the universal proof.

claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: For a nonsingleton top the first advance is mandatory, deletes one level on each side and contributes S. For a singleton top, after covering it, sum over the last level t carrying any lower image: the intervening stays have weight one, and the next advance permits values in the new layer plus the old singleton. Partition those assignments by the nonempty retained subset U; the prefix count summed over U is exactly G_{t,j-1}.
